question_text: Copy the graphs of the following functions and draw the graphs of $y = x$ and $y = f^{-1}(x)$ on the same set of axes. In each case, state the domain and range of both $f$ and $f^{-1}$.

subparts.final_answer: $Domain of $f$: $\{x \mid 0 \leqslant x \leqslant 3\}$, Range of $f$: $\{y \mid -3 \leqslant y \leqslant 0\}$, Domain of $f^{-1}$: $\{x \mid -3 \leqslant x \leqslant 0\}$, Range of $f^{-1}$: $\{y \mid 0 \leqslant y \leqslant 3\}$$

mark_breakdown.desc: Correct domain and range for f
Correct domain and range for f^-1

subparts.solution:
Domain of $f$: $\{x \mid 0 \leqslant x \leqslant 3\}$
Range of $f$: $\{y \mid -3 \leqslant y \leqslant 0\}$
Domain of $f^{-1}$: $\{x \mid -3 \leqslant x \leqslant 0\}$
Range of $f^{-1}$: $\{y \mid 0 \leqslant y \leqslant 3\}$

ai_explanation.concept_rule: Domain is the set of $x$-values, range is the set of $y$-values. For an inverse function, domain and range swap.
step_by_step: From the graph of $f$, $x$ runs from $0$ to $3$, so domain of $f$ is $[0, 3]$.
$y$ runs from $-3$ to $0$, so range of $f$ is $[-3, 0]$.
Swap these to find the domain and range of $f^{-1}$.
ai_explanation.common_pitfalls: Writing interval bounds in the wrong order, e.g., $0 \leqslant y \leqslant -3$.

subparts.final_answer: $Domain of $f$: $\{x \mid -2 \leqslant x \leqslant 1\}$, Range of $f$: $\{y \mid -1 \leqslant y \leqslant 2\}$, Domain of $f^{-1}$: $\{x \mid -1 \leqslant x \leqslant 2\}$, Range of $f^{-1}$: $\{y \mid -2 \leqslant y \leqslant 1\}$$

mark_breakdown.desc: Correct domain and range for f
Correct domain and range for f^-1

subparts.solution:
Domain of $f$: $\{x \mid -2 \leqslant x \leqslant 1\}$
Range of $f$: $\{y \mid -1 \leqslant y \leqslant 2\}$
Domain of $f^{-1}$: $\{x \mid -1 \leqslant x \leqslant 2\}$
Range of $f^{-1}$: $\{y \mid -2 \leqslant y \leqslant 1\}$

ai_explanation.concept_rule: The domain and range of an inverse function are obtained directly by interchanging the domain and range of the original function.
step_by_step: Interchange to get domain of $f^{-1}$ as $[-1, 2]$ and range of $f^{-1}$ as $[-2, 1]$.
ai_explanation.common_pitfalls: Mixing up $x$ and $y$ notation in the set descriptions.

subparts.final_answer: $Domain of $f$: $\{x \mid -3 \leqslant x < 6\}$, Range of $f$: $\{y \mid -1 \leqslant y < 2\}$, Domain of $f^{-1}$: $\{x \mid -1 \leqslant x < 2\}$, Range of $f^{-1}$: $\{y \mid -3 \leqslant y < 6\}$$

mark_breakdown.desc: Correct domain and range for f (including strict inequality at open circle)
Correct domain and range for f^-1

subparts.solution:
Domain of $f$: $\{x \mid -3 \leqslant x < 6\}$
Range of $f$: $\{y \mid -1 \leqslant y < 2\}$
Domain of $f^{-1}$: $\{x \mid -1 \leqslant x < 2\}$
Range of $f^{-1}$: $\{y \mid -3 \leqslant y < 6\}$

ai_explanation.concept_rule: Solid circles denote inclusive endpoints ($\,\leqslant\,$), whereas open circles denote exclusive endpoints ($<$).
step_by_step: The endpoint $(-3, -1)$ is a solid dot, so it is included.
The endpoint $(6, 2)$ is an open circle, so it is excluded.
Domain of $f$ is $[-3, 6)$ and range of $f$ is $[-1, 2)$.
Interchange to find the domain and range of $f^{-1}$.
ai_explanation.common_pitfalls: Using non-strict inequality $\leqslant$ at the open circle.
